Isovolumetric Energy Minimization for Ball-Shaped Volume-Preserving Parameterizations of 3-Manifolds

Shu-Yung Liu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, National Taiwan Normal University, Taipei, Taiwan    Tsung-Ming Huang Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, National Taiwan Normal University, Taipei, Taiwan    Wen-Wei Lin Affiliation: Nanjing Center for Applied Mathematics, Nanjing, China Affiliation: Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan    Mei-Heng Yueh Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, National Taiwan Normal University, Taipei, Taiwan
Abstract

A volume-preserving parameterization is a bijective mapping that maps a 3-manifold onto a specified canonical domain that preserves the local volume. This paper formulates the computation of ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations as an isovolumetric energy minimization (IEM) problem with the boundary points constrained on a unit sphere. In addition, we develop a new preconditioned nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm for solving the IEM problem with guaranteed theoretical convergence and significantly improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms. Applications to solid shape registration and deformation are presented to highlight the usefulness of the proposed algorithm.

Keywords. Simplicial surface, Simplicial mapping, Volume-preserving parameterization, Numerical optimization

AMS subject classifications. 65D18, 68U05, 68U01, 65D17

1 Introduction

The ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterization of a simply connected 3-manifold is a bijective mapping that maps the manifold to a solid unit ball while preserving local volumes. This mapping induces a global coordinate chart for the manifold, simplifying various processing tasks to those applicable to the solid unit ball. Such parameterizations are particularly useful in computational tasks involving complex geometric structures. The technique has been utilized to compute optimal mass transport (OMT) mappings [27], which are subsequently applied to process 3D medical images for brain tumor segmentation [19, 20]. Specifically, unit cube-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations of the brain images are employed in machine-learning applications. The preservation of local volume is crucial for accurately training models to infer the tumor region and measure tumor size.

Recent advanced algorithms for computing 3-manifold mappings include close-to-conformal deformations [5], the simplicial foliation method [4], polycube mappings [13], OMT-based methods [16, 24], scalable locally injective mappings [23], the simplex lifting method [6], foldover-free mappings [14], symmetric volume mappings [1], and the volumetric stretch energy minimization (VSEM) [28, 29, 17]. Among these algorithms, the OMT-based methods and the VSEM aim to compute ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations, similar to this paper. Specifically, the VSEM, which approaches the target mapping through numerical optimization, is the most relevant to our work. In the following, we introduce the pros and cons of the VSEM algorithm.

The volumetric stretch energy was first defined in [28] by heuristically imposing the volume-preserving condition to the volumetric discrete Dirichlet energy. This functional provides a global measurement of volume distortion for mappings, assuming the total volume of the domain and the image are the same. The volumetric stretch energy is equivalent to the sum of the scaled local volumes of tetrahedra with scaling factors being the Jacobian determinant evaluated at those tetrahedra [17]. The theoretical minimal value of the energy is the total image volume, which occurs only at mappings with all local Jacobian determinants being one, i.e., volume-preserving mappings [17]. This concept is a generalization of the stretch energy [30, 26] for surface mappings and can also be extended to higher dimensional manifold mappings.

The previous VSEM algorithm [28, Algorithm 4.4] employed a fixed-point method that iteratively approaches critical points of the functional provided a Dirichlet boundary condition. This method can also be applied to 3-manifolds with boundaries being genus-one surfaces [29]. The boundary mapping in the VSEM algorithm is selected to be a spherical area-preserving mapping achieved by minimizing the stretch energy [30]. The stretch energy for surface mappings is the 2-dimensional analog of the volumetric stretch energy with the theoretical minimal value being the image area. The lower bound of the energy is attained only at area-preserving mappings [26].

The VSEM method is recognized as one of the most effective algorithms for maintaining the volume-preserving property. Still, the VSEM method has room to be improved. The convergence of the VSEM algorithm is not theoretically guaranteed. Also, the choice of fixed spherical area-preserving boundary mappings may not be optimal for ball-shaped volume-preserving mappings. In addition, the original VSEM method [17] assumes the total image volume is constant throughout the iteration process, which may not hold if the boundary points are allowed to glide along the unit sphere. To remedy these drawbacks, in this paper, we express the boundary mapping in spherical coordinates and optimize the whole mapping to find the best ball-shaped parameterization that reaches the least possible value of the objective functional. To compute a minimizer of the objective functional, we apply the nonlinear conjugate gradient (CG) method with suitable preconditioners. An appropriate generalization of the existing theoretical framework of numerical optimization can then guarantee the global convergence of this approach.

1.1 Contribution

This paper improves the problem formulation of the VSEM for computing ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations of simply connected 3-manifolds with robust theoretical support and proposes an efficient algorithm with guaranteed convergence. The main contributions of this paper are listed as follows:

  • (i)

    We formulate the ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations as an isovolumetric energy minimization (IEM) problem with a spherical boundary shape constraint. The main difference between the IEM and the previous VSEM [28] is that the boundary mapping is not prescribed. In other words, the spherical boundary mapping is optimized simultaneously with the interior mapping to reach a parameterization with optimal volume distortions.

  • (ii)

    We deal with the spherical boundary shape constraint by using the spherical coordinates, derive the associated explicit gradient formula, and develop a preconditioned nonlinear CG method for solving the IEM problem.

  • (iii)

    A rigorous proof of the global convergence of the iterations in the proposed algorithm is provided. This proof can be regarded as a generalization of the convergence results for the nonlinear CG method introduced in [22, Chapter 5].

  • (iv)

    Numerical experiments indicate that the effectiveness of decreasing the volume distortions is significantly improved compared to the previous VSEM algorithm [28], one of the most effective methods for computing ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations.

  • (v)

    Applications of ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations to shape registration, deformation, and dissimilarity measurement of human brains are demonstrated to show the practical utility of the proposed algorithm.

1.3 Organization of the paper

The remaining part of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the simplicial 3-manifolds, mappings, and the isovolumetric energy functional. Then, we formulate the IEM problem for ball-shaped mappings and present the explicit formula of the energy gradient in Section 3. The preconditioned nonlinear CG method of the IEM is proposed in Section 4. The associated convergence analysis is provided in Section 5. Numerical experiments and comparisons to the state-of-the-art are presented in Section 6. Applications to volume-preserving registration and deformation are demonstrated in Section 7. Ultimately, concluding remarks are given in Section 8.

2 Simplicial 3-manifolds, mappings, and functionals

We introduce simplicial 3-manifolds, mappings, and the isovolumetric energy functional in subsections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3, respectively.

A simplicial mapping ff is said to be volume-preserving if the volume of each transformed tetrahedron is equal to the original one up to a global constant scaling factor c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, i.e., |f⁡(τ)|=c​|τ||f(\tau)|=c|\tau|, for some c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, for all τ∈𝕋⁡(ℳ)\tau\in\mathbb{T}(\mathcal{M}). The mapping ff is orientation-preserving if c>0c>0, and orientation-reversing if c<0c<0. The mapping ff is called a trivial mapping if c=0c=0. A desirable volume-preserving mapping is one with a nonzero scaling factor, i.e., a nontrivial or a bijective one.

The volumetric stretch energy EVE_{\mathrm{V}} in (3) was defined by Yueh et al. [28] for computing volume-preserving parameterizations of simplicial 3-manifolds. Under the constraint that the total volume of the manifold remains unchanged, Huang et al. [17] further proved that the lower bound of EV​(f)E_{\mathrm{V}}(f) is 𝒱⁡(f)\mathcal{V}(f). The equality holds if and only if the mapping ff is volume-preserving [17, Theorem 3.3]. Based on this fact, it is natural to define the isovolumetric energy as the difference between EV​(f)E_{\mathrm{V}}(f) and 𝒱⁡(f)\mathcal{V}(f). To release the constraint 𝒱⁡(f)=𝒱⁡(e)\mathcal{V}(f)=\mathcal{V}({e}), we scale EV​(f)E_{\mathrm{V}}(f) by the factor 𝒱⁡(e)/𝒱⁡(f)\mathcal{V}({e})/\mathcal{V}(f) in our proposed objective functional (2). In the following theorem, we derive an analogous consequence of [17, Theorem 3.3] without the constant total image volume assumption.

Theorem 1.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a simplicial 33-manifold and ff be a simplicial mapping defined on ℳ\mathcal{M}. The isovolumetric energy in (2) satisfies

EI​(f)≥0,E_{\mathrm{I}}(f)\geq 0,

and the equality holds if and only if ff is volume-preserving.

Proof.

By applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to (2b), we have

EV​(f)​𝒱​(e)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{V}}(f)\,\mathcal{V}({e}) =∑τ∈𝕋⁡(ℳ)|f⁡(τ)|2|τ|​∑τ∈𝕋⁡(ℳ)|τ|≥(∑τ∈𝕋⁡(ℳ)|f⁡(τ)|)2=𝒱​(f)2.\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau\in\mathbb{T}(\mathcal{M})}\frac{|f(\tau)|^{2}}{|\tau|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathbb{T}(\mathcal{M})}|\tau|\geq\left(\sum_{\tau\in\mathbb{T}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\tau)|\right)^{2}=\mathcal{V}(f)^{2}.

𝒱⁡(e)𝒱⁡(f)​EV​(f)≥𝒱⁡(f),\frac{\mathcal{V}({e})}{\mathcal{V}(f)}E_{\mathrm{V}}(f)\geq\mathcal{V}(f),

i.e., the isovolumetric energy (2) satisfies EI​(f)≥0E_{\mathrm{I}}(f)\geq 0. The equality holds if and only if |f⁡(τ)||τ|\frac{|f(\tau)|}{|\tau|} is constant, i.e., ff is volume-preserving. ∎

Theorem 1 provides a robust foundation for computing volume-preserving parameterizations by minimizing the isovolumetric energy (2). Especially when the boundary vertices are allowed to glide along the unit sphere, the exact image volume is not constant.

3 IEM for ball-shaped parameterizations

Recall that a ball-shaped parameterization of a simplicial 3-manifold is a bijective mapping with boundary vertices being mapped to the unit sphere. To remove the spherical constraint for boundary vertices in the objective functional (2), we represent the boundary mapping in spherical coordinates. 4 Preconditioned nonlinear CG method of IEM

Now we demonstrate the preconditioned nonlinear CG method of IEM for ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations.

Note that the target shape is a solid unit ball. To achieve a better mapping, it is natural to perform an anisotropic scaling transformation (AST) to normalize the bounding box of the mesh model before the ball-shaped mapping. Let

𝐯=[v11v12v13vn1vn2vn3]\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{1}^{1}&v_{1}^{2}&v_{1}^{3}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ v_{n}^{1}&v_{n}^{2}&v_{n}^{3}\end{bmatrix}

be the matrix representation of vertex set 𝕍⁡(ℳ)\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{M}) and 𝐜=1n​𝐯⊤​𝟏n\mathbf{c}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{n} be the center of the vertices. The AST Ta:ℝ3→ℝ3T_{a}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is formulated as

Ta​(𝐱)=[r1r2r3]​R​(𝐱−𝐜),T_{a}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}r_{1}\\ &r_{2}\\ &&r_{3}\end{bmatrix}R(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}), (11)

where R∈SO⁡(3)R\in\mathrm{SO}(3) is a suitable rotation and rℓ=1/max1≤s≤n⁡[R⁡(vs−𝐜)]ℓr_{\ell}=1/\max_{1\leq s\leq n}[R(v_{s}-\mathbf{c})]_{\ell}, for ℓ=1,2,3\ell=1,2,3. The matrix RR is chosen to rotate the principal components to the standard Euclidean frame. Let

P=𝐯−𝟏n​𝐜⊤∈ℝn×3P=\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{1}_{n}\mathbf{c}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 3} (12)

be the matrix representation of centralized vertices. Each row of PP is a centralized vertex. The rotation matrix is computed by the singular value decomposition (SVD)

P=U​Σ​V⊤.P=U\Sigma V^{\top}. (13)

The rotation matrix in (11) is then given by R=V⊤R=V^{\top}.

In practice, the initial mapping f(0)f^{(0)} is computed by the fixed-point method of the VSEM in [28, Algorithm 4.4] with a few iteration steps, e.g., 15 steps. At the kkth iteration step, we represent the mapping f(k)f^{(k)} by

𝐟^(k)=[𝐟𝙸1(k)𝐟𝙸2(k)𝐟𝙸3(k)𝜽(k)ϕ(k)].\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{1}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{2}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{3}}^{(k)}\\ {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)}\\ {\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix}. (14)

The corresponding gradient vector

𝐠^(k)≔∇EI​(𝐟^(k))=[∇𝐟𝙸1EI​(f(k))∇𝐟𝙸2EI​(f(k))∇𝐟𝙸3EI​(f(k))∇𝜽EI​(f(k))∇ϕEI​(f(k))]≕[𝐠𝙸1(k)𝐠𝙸2(k)𝐠𝙸3(k)𝐠𝜽(k)𝐠ϕ(k)]\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k)}\coloneqq\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{1}}E_{\mathrm{I}}(f^{(k)})\\ \nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{2}}E_{\mathrm{I}}(f^{(k)})\\ \nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{3}}E_{\mathrm{I}}(f^{(k)})\\ \nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}E_{\mathrm{I}}(f^{(k)})\\ \nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}E_{\mathrm{I}}(f^{(k)})\end{bmatrix}\eqqcolon\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{g}_{\mathtt{I}}^{1}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{g}_{\mathtt{I}}^{2}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{g}_{\mathtt{I}}^{3}}^{(k)}\\ \mathbf{g}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{(k)}\\ \mathbf{g}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix} (15)

is explicitly formulated in (10). For k≥1k\geq 1, we update the interior and boundary mappings along the CG directions with the step length αk\alpha_{k} as

𝐟^(k+1)=𝐟^(k)+αk​𝐩^(k),\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}=\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(k)}, (16a)
where 𝐩^(k)\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(k)} is the CG direction at kkth step given by
𝐩^(k)=[𝐩𝙸1(k)𝐩𝙸2(k)𝐩𝙸3(k)𝐩𝜽(k)𝐩ϕ(k)]=−M−1​𝐠^(k)+βk​𝐩^(k−1).\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(k)}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{p}_{\mathtt{I}}^{1}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{p}_{\mathtt{I}}^{2}}^{(k)}\\ {\mathbf{p}_{\mathtt{I}}^{3}}^{(k)}\\ \mathbf{p}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}^{(k)}\\ \mathbf{p}_{{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix}=-M^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k)}+\beta_{k}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(k-1)}. (16b)
provided that 𝐩^(0)=−M−1​𝐠^(0)\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(0)}=-M^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(0)} and the corrective scalar
βk=𝐠^(k)⊤M−1𝐠^(k)𝐠^(k−1)⊤M−1𝐠^(k−1)\beta_{k}=\frac{{\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k)}}{}^{\top}M^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k)}}{{\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k-1)}}{}^{\top}M^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{g}}^{(k-1)}} (16c)

M=[I3⊗[LV​(f(0))]𝙸,𝙸I2⊗[LV​(f(0))]𝙱,𝙱].M=\begin{bmatrix}I_{3}\otimes[L_{\mathrm{V}}(f^{(0)})]_{\mathtt{I},\mathtt{I}}\\ &I_{2}\otimes[L_{\mathrm{V}}(f^{(0)})]_{\mathtt{B},\mathtt{B}}\end{bmatrix}.

In practice, we computed the preordered Cholesky decomposition so that linear systems of [LV​(f(0))]𝙸,𝙸[L_{\mathrm{V}}(f^{(0)})]_{\mathtt{I},\mathtt{I}} and [LV​(f(0))]𝙱,𝙱[L_{\mathrm{V}}(f^{(0)})]_{\mathtt{B},\mathtt{B}} can be efficiently solved by forward and backward substitutions.

To estimate the optimal step length αk\alpha_{k}, we define Φ(k)​(α):ℝ→ℝ\Phi^{(k)}(\alpha):\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as

Φ(k)​(α)=EI​(𝐟^(k)+α​𝐩^(k)),\Phi^{(k)}(\alpha)=E_{I}\big(\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}+\alpha\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{(k)}\big),

However, it is not feasible due to the nonlinearity of the Laplacian matrix (3b). Instead, we approximate Φ(k)\Phi^{(k)} by a quadratic function Φq(k)\Phi_{q}^{(k)} as

which satisfies

{Φq(k)​(0)=Φ(k)​(0)=EI​(𝐟^(k)),dd​αΦq(k)(0)=dd​αΦ(k)(0)=𝐩(k)⊤∇EI(𝐟^(k)),Φq(k)​(αk−1)=Φ(k)​(αk−1)=EI​(𝐟^(k)+αk−1​𝐩^(k)).\begin{cases}\Phi_{q}^{(k)}(0)=\Phi^{(k)}(0)=E_{\mathrm{I}}\big(\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\big),\\ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi_{q}^{(k)}(0)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0)={{\mathbf{p}}^{(k)}}^{\top}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}\big(\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\big),\\ \Phi_{q}^{(k)}(\alpha_{k-1})=\Phi^{(k)}(\alpha_{k-1})=E_{\mathrm{I}}\big(\widehat{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}+\alpha_{k-1}{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}}^{(k)}\big).\end{cases}

The coefficients aka_{k}, bkb_{k}, and ckc_{k} are thus can be computed by

ak\displaystyle a_{k} =Φ(k)(0),bk=dd​αΦ(k)(0), and \displaystyle=\Phi^{(k)}(0),~~~b_{k}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0),~\text{ and }~
ck\displaystyle c_{k} =1αk−12​(Φ(k)​(αk−1)−Φ(k)​(0)−αk−1​dd​α​Φ(k)​(0)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{k-1}^{2}}\Big(\Phi^{(k)}(\alpha_{k-1})-\Phi^{(k)}(0)-\alpha_{k-1}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0)\Big).

αk=−dd​α​Φ(k)​(0)2​ak=−αk−12​dd​α​Φ(k)​(0)2​(Φ(k)​(αk−1)−Φ(k)​(0)−αk−1​dd​α​Φ(k)​(0)).\alpha_{k}=\frac{-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0)}{2a_{k}}=\frac{-\alpha_{k-1}^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0)}{2\big(\Phi^{(k)}(\alpha_{k-1})-\Phi^{(k)}(0)-\alpha_{k-1}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}\Phi^{(k)}(0)\big)}. The detailed computational procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

5 Convergence analysis of IEM algorithm

In this section, we provide the proof in detail for the global convergence of the proposed IEM, Algorithm 1. The consequence of the main theorem (Theorem 2) is a generalization of the convergence of the nonlinear CG method introduced in [22, Chapter 5]. Similar techniques have been applied in the convergence analysis of the authalic energy minimization for disk area-preserving parameterizations [21]. One of the main differences is that we change the definition of the denominator of cos⁡θM(k)\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)} in the modified Zoutendijk’s condition (Lemma 4) so that the proof of Theorem 2 would be simpler. For simplicity, in the remaining part of this section, we denote 𝐟^\widehat{\mathbf{f}} in (14), 𝐠^\widehat{\mathbf{g}} in (15), and 𝐩^\widehat{\mathbf{p}} in (16b) as 𝐟\mathbf{f}, 𝐠\mathbf{g}, and 𝐩\mathbf{p}, respectively.

The global convergence of Algorithm 1 is theoretically guaranteed under the assumption that each step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions

EI​(𝐟(k)+αk​𝐩(k))\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}) ≤EI(𝐟(k))+c1αk∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k),\displaystyle\leq E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})+c_{1}\alpha_{k}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}, (18a)
|∇EI(𝐟(k)+αk𝐩(k))⊤𝐩(k)|\displaystyle|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}\mathbf{p}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}| ≤c2|∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)|,\displaystyle\leq c_{2}|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}|, (18b)

with 0<c1<c2<120<c_{1}<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}. The existence of each desirable step length αk\alpha_{k} is guaranteed by Lemma 2 under the assumption that 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is a descent direction of EIE_{\mathrm{I}} at 𝐟(k)\mathbf{f}^{(k)}.

In the following lemma, we prove the Lipschitz continuities of the objective functional and its gradient with respect to the vertex image, which play crucial roles in the proof of the convergence of IEM.

Lemma 1.

The isovolumetric energy EIE_{\mathrm{I}} (2) and its gradient ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}} are Lipschitz continuous.

Proof.

Similar to the matrix representation 𝐟\mathbf{f} of a simplicial mapping ff in (1), it can also be represented as a vector (𝐟1⊤,𝐟2⊤,𝐟3⊤)⊤({\mathbf{f}^{1}}^{\top},{\mathbf{f}^{2}}^{\top},{\mathbf{f}^{3}}^{\top})^{\top} of length 3​n3n, provided that nn is the number of vertices of the triangular mesh model. The objective functional EIE_{\mathrm{I}} of ball-shaped simplicial mapping can then be represented a function EI:[−1,1]3​n→ℝE_{\mathrm{I}}:[-1,1]^{3n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} defined on a compact subset [−1,1]3​n[-1,1]^{3n} of ℝ3​n\mathbb{R}^{3n} as

EI​(f)≡EI​(𝐟)≡EI​(f11,…,fn1,f12,…,fn2,f13,…,fn3).E_{\mathrm{I}}(f)\equiv E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f})\equiv E_{\mathrm{I}}(f_{1}^{1},\ldots,f_{n}^{1},f_{1}^{2},\ldots,f_{n}^{2},f_{1}^{3},\ldots,f_{n}^{3}).

Then, for every ball-shaped simplicial mappings 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐲∈[−1,1]3​n\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1]^{3n}, we define ϕ⁡(t)=EI​((1−t)​𝐱+t​𝐲)\phi(t)=E_{\mathrm{I}}((1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{y}). Since EIE_{\mathrm{I}} is smooth, by the mean value theorem, there exists a value ξ1∈(0,1)\xi_{1}\in(0,1) such that 𝐳1=(1−ξ1)​𝐱+ξ1​𝐲\mathbf{z}_{1}=(1-\xi_{1})\mathbf{x}+\xi_{1}\mathbf{y} and

EI(𝐲)−EI(𝐱)=ϕ(1)−ϕ(0)=ϕ′(ξ1)=∇EI(𝐳1)⊤(𝐲−𝐱).E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x})=\phi(1)-\phi(0)=\phi^{\prime}(\xi_{1})=\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{z}_{1})^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}).

Since the domain of EIE_{\mathrm{I}} is compact,

‖EI​(𝐲)−EI​(𝐱)‖≤C1​‖𝐲−𝐱‖,\|E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x})\|\leq C_{1}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|,

where C1=max𝐟∈[−1,1]3​n⁡‖∇EI​(𝐟)‖C_{1}=\max_{\mathbf{f}\in[-1,1]^{3n}}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f})\| is finite, i.e., EIE_{\mathrm{I}} is Lipschitz continuous.

On the other hand, to show the Lipschitz continuity of ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}, we define φ(t)=(∇EI(𝐲)−∇EI(𝐱))⊤∇EI((1−t)𝐱+t𝐲)\varphi(t)=(\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x}))^{\top}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}((1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{y}). Since ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}} is smooth, by the mean value theorem, there exists a value ξ2∈(0,1)\xi_{2}\in(0,1) such that 𝐳2=(1−ξ2)​𝐱+ξ2​𝐲\mathbf{z}_{2}=(1-\xi_{2})\mathbf{x}+\xi_{2}\mathbf{y} and

‖∇EI​(𝐲)−∇EI​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x})\|^{2} =φ⁡(1)−φ⁡(0)=φ′​(ξ2)\displaystyle=\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)=\varphi^{\prime}(\xi_{2})
=(∇EI​(𝐲)−∇EI​(𝐱))⊤​∇2EI​(𝐳2)​(𝐲−𝐱).\displaystyle=(\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x}))^{\top}\nabla^{2}E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{z}_{2})(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}).

Since the domain of EIE_{\mathrm{I}} is compact,

‖∇EI​(𝐲)−∇EI​(𝐱)‖2≤C2​‖∇EI​(𝐲)−∇EI​(𝐱)‖​‖𝐲−𝐱‖,\displaystyle\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}\leq C_{2}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{y})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{x})\|\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|,

where C2=max𝐟∈[−1,1]3​n⁡‖∇2EI​(𝐟)‖C_{2}=\max_{\mathbf{f}\in[-1,1]^{3n}}\|\nabla^{2}E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f})\| is finite, i.e., ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}} is Lipschitz continuous. ∎

To guarantee the energy EIE_{\mathrm{I}} decreases sufficiently at the kkth iteration step, we require not only the descent direction 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)}, but also a proper step length αk\alpha_{k} that satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions (18). Since EIE_{\mathrm{I}} is bounded below, the following lemma guarantees the existence of such desirable step lengths.

Lemma 2 ([22, Lemma 3.1]).

Intervals of step lengths that satisfy the strong Wolfe conditions (18) always exist, provided that 0<c1<c2<10<c_{1}<c_{2}<1 and 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is a descent direction at 𝐟(k)\mathbf{f}^{(k)}.

For k=0k=0, since M−1M^{-1} is symmetric positive definite, 𝐩(0)=−M−1​𝐠(0)\mathbf{p}^{(0)}=-M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(0)} is a descent direction, and thus the existence of a desirable step length α(0)\alpha^{(0)} satisfying (18) is guaranteed by Lemma 2. To keep 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} being the descent direction for k≥1k\geq 1, the constant c2c_{2} should be chosen in (0,12)(0,\frac{1}{2}). The following lemma, a variant of [22, Lemma 5.6], provides crucial bounds of the value ∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−12\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}, which serves as a core step for the proof of the global convergence of the IEM.

Lemma 3.

Let MM be a symmetric positive definite matrix. Suppose the step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions (18). Then, the vector 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} satisfies

−11−c2≤∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−12≤2​c2−11−c2,-\frac{1}{1-c_{2}}\leq\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}\leq\frac{2c_{2}-1}{1-c_{2}}, (19)

for all k≥0k\geq 0, where ∥⋅∥M−1\|\cdot\|_{M^{-1}} denotes the M−1M^{-1}-norm defined as ‖𝐯‖M−1=𝐯⊤​M−1​𝐯.\|\mathbf{v}\|_{M^{-1}}=\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{v}}.

Proof.

We prove (19) by induction on kk. For k=0k=0, since 𝐩(0)=−M−1​𝐠(0)\mathbf{p}^{(0)}=-M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(0)}, we have

∇EI(𝐟(0))⊤𝐩(0)‖∇EI​(𝐟(0))‖M−12=−𝐠(0)⊤​M−1​𝐠(0)𝐠(0)⊤​M−1​𝐠(0)=−1,\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(0)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(0)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(0)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}=\frac{-{\mathbf{g}^{(0)}}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(0)}}{{\mathbf{g}^{(0)}}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(0)}}=-1,

which satisfies (19). Assume the induction hypothesis (19) holds for k=nk=n. Then, for k=n+1k=n+1, with (16b) and (16c), we have

∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n+1)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n+1))‖M−12\displaystyle\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n+1)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}} =−𝐠(n+1)⊤​M−1​𝐠(n+1)𝐠(n+1)⊤​M−1​𝐠(n+1)+βn+1​∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n+1))‖M−12\displaystyle=\frac{-{\mathbf{g}^{(n+1)}}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(n+1)}}{{\mathbf{g}^{(n+1)}}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(n+1)}}+\beta_{n+1}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}
=−1+𝐠(n+1)⊤​M−1​𝐠(n+1)𝐠(n)⊤​M−1​𝐠(n)​∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n)𝐠(n+1)⊤​M−1​𝐠(n+1)=−1+∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n))‖M−12.\displaystyle=-1+\frac{{{\mathbf{g}}^{(n+1)}}^{\top}M^{-1}{\mathbf{g}}^{(n+1)}}{{\mathbf{g}^{(n)}}^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf{g}^{(n)}}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}}{{{\mathbf{g}}^{(n+1)}}^{\top}M^{-1}{\mathbf{g}}^{(n+1)}}=-1+\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}. (20)

Then, the second Wolfe condition (18b) implies |∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n)|≤−c2∇EI(𝐟(n))⊤𝐩(n),|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}|\leq-c_{2}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}, i.e.,

c2∇EI(𝐟(n))⊤𝐩(n)≤∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n)≤−c2∇EI(𝐟(n))⊤𝐩(n).\displaystyle c_{2}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}\leq\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}\leq-c_{2}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}. (21)

As a result, from (20) and (21), we have

−1+c2​∇EI(𝐟(n))⊤𝐩(n)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n))‖M−12\displaystyle-1+c_{2}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}} ≤∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n+1)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n+1))‖M−12≤−1−c2​∇EI(𝐟(n))⊤𝐩(n)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n))‖M−12.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n+1)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}\leq-1-c_{2}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}.

Then, from the induction hypothesis (19) with k=nk=n, we have

−11−c2=−1−c21−c2≤∇EI(𝐟(n+1))⊤𝐩(n+1)‖∇EI​(𝐟(n+1))‖M−12≤−1+c21−c2=2​c2−11−c2,-\frac{1}{1-c_{2}}=-1-\frac{c_{2}}{1-c_{2}}\leq\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(n+1)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(n+1)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}\leq-1+\frac{c_{2}}{1-c_{2}}=\frac{2c_{2}-1}{1-c_{2}},

i.e., (19) holds for k=n+1k=n+1. ∎

By applying Lemma 3 with a value c2c_{2} chosen in (0,12)(0,\frac{1}{2}), the vector 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} could be guaranteed to be a descent direction of EIE_{I} at 𝐟(k){\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}, which is introduced in the following corollary.

Corollary 1.

Let MM be a symmetric positive definite matrix. Suppose the step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions (18) with 0<c2<120<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}. Then, 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is a descent direction of EIE_{I} at 𝐟(k){\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}.

Proof.

We define a monotonically increasing function φ⁡(x)=2​x−11−x\varphi(x)=\frac{2x-1}{1-x} on [0,12][0,\frac{1}{2}] with φ⁡(0)=−1\varphi(0)=-1 and φ⁡(12)=0\varphi(\frac{1}{2})=0. Then, the second inequality of (19) with 0<c2<120<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2} implies

∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−12≤2​c2−11−c2=φ⁡(c2)<φ⁡(12)=0.\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|^{2}_{M^{-1}}}\leq\frac{2c_{2}-1}{1-c_{2}}=\varphi(c_{2})<\varphi(\textstyle\frac{1}{2})=0.

Thus, ∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)<0\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}<0, and hence 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is a descent direction of EIE_{I} at 𝐟(k){\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}. ∎

For each iteration of the IEM algorithm, Corollary 1 and Lemma 2 guarantee the existence of step lengths satisfying the strong Wolfe condition (18) with 0<c1<c2<120<c_{1}<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}. The Lipschitz continuities of EIE_{\mathrm{I}} and ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}} could be applied to describe further the directional difference between 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} and ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}, which is a variant of the Zoutendijk’s condition and serves as a core stone for the proof of the global convergence of the preconditioned nonlinear CG method of the IEM.

Lemma 4 (modified Zoutendijk’s condition).

Let MM be a symmetric positive definite matrix. Suppose the step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions (18) with 0<c1<c2<120<c_{1}<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}. Then,

∑k=0∞cos2⁡θM(k)​‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−12<∞,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^{2}\theta_{M}^{(k)}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}}^{2}<\infty, (22a)
where cos⁡θM(k)\cos\theta^{(k)}_{M} is defined as
cos⁡θM(k)=−∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−1​‖𝐩(k)‖M,\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)}=-\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}}\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}}, (22b)
provided that 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is given by (16).
Proof.

The step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the Wolfe condition (18), by Corollary 1, 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is a descent direction and thus the second Wolfe condition (18b) holds, i.e.,

∇EI(𝐟(k+1))⊤𝐩(k)≥c2∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k).\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\geq c_{2}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}. (23)

By subtracting ∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)} to both sides of (23), we obtain

(∇EI(𝐟(k+1))−∇EI(𝐟(k)))⊤𝐩(k)≥(c2−1)∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k).\big(\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\big)^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\geq(c_{2}-1)\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}. (24)

Since ∇EI\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}} is Lipschitz continuous, (24) implies

(c2−1)∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)≤∥∇EI(𝐟(k+1))−∇EI(𝐟(k))∥∥𝐩(k)∥≤C∥𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k)∥∥𝐩(k)∥.(c_{2}-1)\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\leq\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)})-\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|\leq C\,\|{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\|\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|. (25)

The values in (25) can be estimated in MM-norm as

∥𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k)∥=∥M−1/2(𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k))∥M≤∥M−1/2∥M∥𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k)∥M,\|{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\|=\|M^{-1/2}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M}\leq\|M^{-1/2}\|_{M}\|{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\|_{M}, (26)

and

∥𝐩(k)∥=∥M−1/2𝐩(k)∥M≤∥M−1/2∥M∥𝐩(k)∥M.\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|=\|M^{-1/2}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}\leq\|M^{-1/2}\|_{M}\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}. (27)

From (23)–(26), we have

αk=‖𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k)‖M‖𝐩(k)‖M=‖𝐟(k+1)−𝐟(k)‖M​‖𝐩(k)‖M‖𝐩(k)‖M2≥c2−1C∥M−1/2∥2M​∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖𝐩(k)‖M2.\alpha_{k}=\frac{\|{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\|_{M}}{\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}}=\frac{\|{\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}-{\mathbf{f}}^{(k)}\|_{M}\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}}{\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|_{M}^{2}}\geq\frac{c_{2}-1}{C\|M^{-1/2}\|^{2}_{M}}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|^{2}_{M}}. (28)

By substituting (28) into the first Wolfe condition (18a), we obtain

EI​(𝐟(k+1))\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}) ≤EI(𝐟(k))−c11−c2C∥M−1/2∥2M∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)‖𝐩(k)‖M2∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k)\displaystyle\leq E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})-c_{1}\frac{1-c_{2}}{C\,\|M^{-1/2}\|^{2}_{M}}\frac{\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}}{\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|^{2}_{M}}\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)}
≤EI​(𝐟(k))−C~​(∇EI(𝐟(k))⊤𝐩(k))2‖𝐩(k)‖M2=EI​(𝐟(k))−C~​cos2⁡θM(k)​‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−12,\displaystyle\leq E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})-\widetilde{C}\frac{(\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{p}^{(k)})^{2}}{\|\mathbf{p}^{(k)}\|^{2}_{M}}=E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})-\widetilde{C}\cos^{2}\theta_{M}^{(k)}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}}^{2}, (29)

where C~=c1​(1−c2)C∥M−1/2∥2M>0\widetilde{C}=\frac{c_{1}(1-c_{2})}{C\,\|M^{-1/2}\|^{2}_{M}}>0 and cos⁡θM(k)\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)} is defined as (22b). The recursive inequality (29) implies

EI​(𝐟(k+1))≤EI​(𝐟(0))−C~​∑j=0kcos2⁡θM(j)​‖∇EI​(𝐟(j))‖M−12.E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)})\leq E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(0)})-\widetilde{C}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\cos^{2}\theta_{M}^{(j)}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(j)})\|_{M^{-1}}^{2}.

In other words,

∑j=0kcos2⁡θM(j)​‖∇EI​(𝐟(j))‖M−12=1C~​(EI​(𝐟(0))−EI​(𝐟(k+1))).\sum_{j=0}^{k}\cos^{2}\theta_{M}^{(j)}\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(j)})\|_{M^{-1}}^{2}=\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}}\big(E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(0)})-E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)})\big). (30)

Since EI​(𝐟)≥0E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}})\geq 0 is bounded below, the value EI​(𝐟(0))−EI​(𝐟(k+1))E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(0)})-E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k+1)}) in (30) is bounded above. Therefore,

limk→∞∑j=0kcos2⁡θM(j)≤sup𝐟1C~​(EI​(𝐟(0))−EI​(𝐟))<∞,\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\cos^{2}\theta_{M}^{(j)}\leq\sup_{\mathbf{f}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}}\big(E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(0)})-E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}})\big)<\infty,

which is equivalent to (22). ∎

Lemma 4 would guarantee the global convergence of the iteration if 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} is parallel to ∇E​(𝐟(k))\nabla E(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}) in M−1M^{-1}-norm, i.e. 𝐩(k)=−M−1∇E(𝐟(k))\mathbf{p}^{(k)}=-M^{-1}\nabla E(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}), since cos⁡θM(k)=1\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)}=1. For the nonlinear CG method with preconditioners, the correction term makes 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)} deviate from the vector −M−1∇E(𝐟(k))-M^{-1}\nabla E(\mathbf{f}^{(k)}) while cos⁡θM(k)>0\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)}>0 due to descent direction 𝐩(k)\mathbf{p}^{(k)}. To guarantee that ‖∇E​(𝐟(k))‖M−1\|\nabla E(\mathbf{f}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}} vanishes as kk tends to infinite, in the following theorem, we apply the first inequality of (19) in Lemma 3 to show that cos⁡θM(k)\cos\theta_{M}^{(k)} would not vanish and establish the global convergence of the iteration of IEM.

Theorem 2.

Suppose the step length αk\alpha_{k} satisfies the strong Wolfe conditions (18) with 0<c1<c2<120<c_{1}<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}. Then,

lim infk→∞‖∇EI​(𝐟(k))‖M−1=0,\liminf_{k\to\infty}{\|\nabla E_{\mathrm{I}}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}}}=0, (31)

provided that MM is a symmetric positive definite matrix.

Proof.

We prove (31) by contradiction. Assume on the contrary that

lim infk→∞‖∇EA​(𝐟(k))‖M−1≠0,\liminf_{k\to\infty}{\|\nabla{E}_{A}({\mathbf{f}}^{(k)})\|_{M^{-1}}}\neq 0,

i.e., there is a natural number NN and a positive real number γ\gamma such that

The global convergence of the proposed IEM (Algorithm 1) is directly guaranteed by Theorem 2, which is summarized in the following corollary.

Corollary 2.

Assume each step length satisfying the strong Wolfe conditions (18) with 0<c1<c2<120<c_{1}<c_{2}<\frac{1}{2}, the preconditioned nonlinear CG method, Algorithm 1 converges globally.

6 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we present the numerical results of the proposed preconditioned nonlinear CG method for IEM, Algorithm 1. The benchmark tetrahedral mesh models demonstrated in Figure 3 are from Jacobson’s GitHub [18], Gu’s website [15], and the BraTS databases [2, 3]. Some tetrahedral mesh models are generated by using the iso2mesh [12, 25] and JIGSAW mesh generators [8, 7, 9, 10, 11]. All the experiments are performed in MATLAB on a laptop with AMD Ryzen 9 5900HS and 32 GB RAM.

To quantify the local volume distortion of a mapping ff, we compute the relative difference between the volumes of τ\tau and f⁡(τ)f(\tau) as

DV​(f,τ)=||f⁡(τ)|/𝒱⁡(f)−|τ|/𝒱⁡(e)|τ|/𝒱⁡(e)|.D_{\mathrm{V}}(f,\tau)=\left|\frac{|f(\tau)|/\mathcal{V}(f)-|\tau|/\mathcal{V}(e)}{|\tau|/\mathcal{V}(e)}\right|. (45)

A volume-preserving mapping ff has the property that DV​(f,τ)=0D_{\mathrm{V}}(f,\tau)=0, for every τ∈𝕋⁡(ℳ)\tau\in\mathbb{T}(\mathcal{M}).

Figure 4 demonstrates the histograms of the local volume distortions (45) of the mappings computed by the proposed IEM, Algorithm 1 with 500 iterations. It shows that most of the relative volume differences produced by the mappings are less than 0.1. Table 1 further shows the 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles of DV​(f,τ)D_{\mathrm{V}}(f,\tau) (45), respectively. In particular, the 95th percentile indicates that at least 95%95\% tetrahedra have local distortions of the magnitude 10−210^{-2} in volume ratios, which is quite satisfactory.

6.1 Comparison to the state-of-the-art

To the best of our knowledge, the fixed-point method of the VSEM [28, Algorithm 4.4] is the state-of-the-art method with the best effectiveness and accuracy for computing ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations of simplicial 3-manifolds. Comparison of the VSEM [28, Algorithm 4.4] to another state-of-the-art method, the OMT-based method [24, Algorithm 4], can be found in [28, Section 6], which indicates that the VSEM is significantly more effective and accurate than the OMT-based method [24, Algorithm 4] on computing ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations.

In this subsection, we compare the proposed IEM, Algorithm 1, to the fixed-point method of the VSEM [28, Algorithm 4.4]. The number of iterations for both algorithms is set to 500. The initial mapping is computed by the fixed-point method of VSEM [28] with 15 iterations.

The relationship between the isovolumetric energy and the number of iterations is demonstrated in Figure 5, which indicates that the proposed IEM is significantly more effective in decreasing the energy (2).

In addition, the mean and standard deviation (SD) of local volume distortion (45), the isovolumetric energy EIE_{I} (2), and the number of folding tetrahedra of resulting mappings are further demonstrated in Table 2 and visualized in Figures 6 and 7. We observe that our proposed IEM has significant improvement in terms of accuracy and bijectivity. On average, our proposed IEM improves 53%53\%, 26%26\%, and 38%38\%, in terms of energy, mean, and SD of local volume distortion, respectively, relative to that of the fixed-point method of the VSEM [28, Algorithm 4.4].

Furthermore, we compare the computational time costs of the proposed IEM and the VSEM [28] in Figure 6. The results are consistent with the computational complexity of O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) for both algorithms. This indicates that the efficiency of the proposed IEM is competitive with that of the VSEM [28].

On the other hand, to present the utility of the AST (11) on improving the bijectivity, in Table 3, we further demonstrate the numerical results in the above metrics without performing the AST (11) in Steps 3–5 of Algorithm 1. Comparing the results in Table 3 to those with the AST in Table 2, we observe that the volume-preserving qualities are similar in both tables. However, the bijectivity of mappings produced by the proposed IEM is significantly improved and achieves completely bijective mappings. These results demonstrate the great utility of the AST (11) in enhancing the bijectivity in the proposed IEM.

The comparison between the number of folding tetrahedra with and without performing the AST for five particular models is further visualized in Figure 8, which indicates that the AST (11) shows little utility in improving the bijectivity of mappings produced by the fixed-point method [28] of VSEM. These results indicate that both the boundary updating and the AST (11) are crucial in achieving bijective volume-preserving ball-shaped mappings. To the best of our knowledge, there is no algorithm for tetrahedral mappings that could theoretically guarantee the bijectivity of the produced mapping. Still, numerical results of the proposed IEM indicate that the volume-preserving property might potentially provide a way to achieve orientation-preserving tetrahedral mappings.

7 Applications to shape registration and deformation

The ball-shaped parameterization computed by the IEM is unique up to a rotation transformation. Based on this fact, each rotation transformation in the parameter space defines a volume-preserving registration mapping between manifolds. A natural one-to-one correspondence between two manifolds can then be obtained through an optimal rotation transformation in the parameter space. This mapping also provides a measurement of shape dissimilarity between the manifolds.

In practice, to find the volume-preserving registration mapping between two tetrahedral meshes ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} and ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1}, we first compute the volume-preserving parameterizations fs:ℳs→𝔹3f_{s}:\mathcal{M}_{s}\to\mathbb{B}^{3}, s=0,1s=0,1, using Algorithm 1. The remaining degrees of freedom on the solid unit ball are rotation transformations in SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3). To remove such a freedom, we compute the optimal rotations by

gs=argming∈SO⁡(3)∑v∈𝕍⁡(ℳs)∥g∘fs(v)−v∥22vol(v),s=0,1,g_{s}=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{g\in\mathrm{SO}(3)}\sum_{v\in\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{M}_{s})}\|g\circ f_{s}(v)-v\|_{2}^{2}\,\mathrm{vol}(v),~s=0,1,

where vol⁡(v)\mathrm{vol}(v) denotes the vertex volume of vv defined by vol⁡(v)=14​∑τ∋v|τ|\mathrm{vol}(v)=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\tau\ni v}|\tau|. Then, the rigid registration mapping on 𝔹3\mathbb{B}^{3} is given by h=g1−1∘g0h=g_{1}^{-1}\circ g_{0}. Ultimately, the volume-preserving registration mapping φ:ℳ0→ℳ1\varphi:\mathcal{M}_{0}\to\mathcal{M}_{1} is given by φ=f1−1∘h∘f0\varphi=f_{1}^{-1}\circ h\circ f_{0}, as illustrated in Figure 9.

To visualize the deformation of the mapping φ\varphi, one can employ the linear homotopy, defined as

ℋ⁡(v,t)=(1−t)​v+t​φ​(v).\mathcal{H}(v,t)=(1-t)v+t\varphi(v). (46)

In Figure 10, we demonstrate the simplicial 33-manifolds ℋ⁡(ℳ0,t)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{M}_{0},t), for t=0,13,23t=0,\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}, and 11, which shows that the deformation is very subtle because the shapes of two given simplicial 33-manifolds are similar. To quantify the deformation resulting from φ\varphi, we compute the value

d⁡(φ)=∑v∈𝕍⁡(ℳ0)‖v−φ⁡(v)‖2​vol​(v)|ℳ0|=7.82%,d(\varphi)=\frac{\sum_{v\in\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{M}_{0})}\|v-\varphi(v)\|_{2}\mathrm{vol}(v)}{|\mathcal{M}_{0}|}=7.82\%,

which is reasonably small.

8 Concluding remarks

In this paper, we have formulated the computation of ball-shaped volume-preserving parameterizations as a nonlinear functional minimization problem and developed an efficient preconditioned nonlinear CG method for solving the problem. Convergence analysis is provided to guarantee the global convergence of the proposed algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy and computational efficiency compared to a previous representative state-of-the-art algorithm. Additionally, our algorithm shows considerable potential for measuring shape dissimilarity, an essential issue in shape analysis. This highlights the practical utility and effectiveness of our developed IEM algorithm.
